scenes.title: Cold open
narration: At dawn, the dancer collapses in a trance after 'destroying' a theatrical play, only to be revived by temple holy water.
This is Veerabhadra. Ancient/Medieval origin; documented in modern Goa.
on_screen: Title card: Veerabhadra · India · Ancient/Medieval origin; documented in modern Goa

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is believed to have migrated from Karnataka to Goa, evidenced by its Kannada (Kanadi) proclamations and structural similarities to traditions in Tumkur.
It is deeply rooted in the Shaivite tradition, specifically the myth of Veerabhadra's creation to avenge the goddess Sati.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed annually during the Shigmo festival and on Chaitra Poornima (full moon).
It signifies the destruction of Daksha's Yajna (Daksha Yajna Vansa), representing the divine intervention of Shiva.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dancer carries an unsheathed sword in each hand, executing rhythmic cycles that simulate a battle.
While stationary during proclamations, the dancer moves his head in sync with the 'Horavani' chants.
Upon entering the temple mandap, the movements become more aggressive and expansive to mimic the destruction of the Yajna.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is driven by traditional musical instruments and the 'Horavani' proclamation led by a 'murveli'.
The crowd provides a vocal rhythmic response with the phrase 'Ha Udo'.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The attire includes a flared waist cloth, demonic ornaments, and a Mysorean turban.
A 'prabhavali' (bamboo halo) is tied to the back.
Face makeup is styled after Kathakali.
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: The role is traditionally inherited by a male performer from a specific family lineage; in Sanguem, it is performed specifically in front of the Kosambe family residence.
In Sanquelim, the dance includes a theatrical drama component where actors flee from the dancer.
The tradition follows a Kannada (Kanadi) lineage, maintaining linguistic and stylistic links to the Veerbhadra practices of Karnataka.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dancer must observe a three-day vow of fasting and isolation. Only specific families may inherit the role.
